content: In 2022, it was noted that the bioavailability of delamanid may be altered if the 50 mg tablet is split, crushed, or dissolved. Delamanid is sensitive to oxidation and heat, so storing pill fragments for later use may lead to reduced delivery of the active compound and the formation of unspecified oxidation by-products. Avoiding injectable-containing regimens is particularly important in children, especially those who are very young or have mild disease (as indicated by the absence of malnutrition, severe extrapulmonary disease, cavitation on chest radiography, or HIV infection). Hearing loss in children can have a permanent impact on language acquisition and learning abilities. Therefore, if amikacin or streptomycin is used in children, regular audiometry is required. Recommendations for treatment duration also apply to children, with adjustments based on treatment response. Shortening the total treatment duration to less than 18 months may be considered for children without extensive disease. For extrapulmonary tuberculosis (TB) and TB meningitis, the WHO recommendations for longer multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) regimens also apply, with adjustments based on the specific disease location. Treatment of MDR/RR-TB meningitis should be guided by drug susceptibility testing (DST) of the infecting strain and knowledge of TB medications that cross the blood-brain barrier. Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ethionamide, prothionamide, cycloserine, terizidone, linezolid, and imipenem-cilastatin penetrate the central nervous system (CNS) well. However, seizures may be more common in children with meningitis treated with imipenem-cilastatin, so meropenem is preferred in such cases. High-dose isoniazid and pyrazinamide can also reach therapeutic levels in cerebrospinal fluid and may be useful if the strains are susceptible. In contrast, para-aminosalicylic acid and ethambutol do not penetrate the CNS well and should not be relied upon for MDR/RR-TB meningitis. Amikacin and streptomycin penetrate the CNS only in the presence of meningeal inflammation. There is limited data on the CNS penetration of clofazimine, bedaquiline, or delamanid, and cerebrospinal fluid concentrations may not reflect levels in the meninges or brain. During pregnancy, amikacin, streptomycin, prothionamide, and ethionamide are generally contraindicated. Knowledge about the safety of bedaquiline and delamanid during pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited. However, observational data from South Africa involving 58 pregnant women treated with bedaquiline showed no significant differences in infant outcomes, pregnancy outcomes, or maternal treatment outcomes, including infant weight gain up to one year of age. In such cases, individualized regimens with better-established safety profiles are recommended. Outcomes of treatment and pregnancy, including postpartum surveillance for congenital anomalies, should be documented to inform future recommendations for MDR-TB treatment during pregnancy. The concurrent use of bedaquiline and delamanid has insufficient evidence to assess efficacy or effectiveness. However, safety data suggest no additional safety concerns. These drugs may be used in patients with limited treatment options, such as those with extensive drug resistance or intolerance to other second-line TB medications. Safety monitoring, including ECG and electrolyte monitoring, is essential when using these medications, especially given their potential to prolong the QT interval. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of DST to maximize the effectiveness of MDR/RR-TB regimens. Rapid diagnostic testing can help clinicians determine eligibility for specific regimens and select appropriate agents. Empirical treatment may be initiated if DST results are unavailable, with adjustments made once results are obtained. When DST indicates resistance to an agent, it is better to replace that agent, even for drugs with unreliable DST methods. The 2018 guideline update revised weight-based dosage schedules for MDR-TB regimens for both children and adults, based on the latest knowledge about optimal drug use. Adherence to these schedules is advised. Treatment interruption should be avoided to increase the likelihood of success, and patient adherence can be supported through health facility visits, home visits, or digital communication technologies. Patients on longer MDR-TB regimens require monitoring for treatment response and safety through clinical and laboratory testing. This includes history-taking, physical examination, chest radiography, audiometry, visual acuity tests, and electrocardiography. Monitoring bacteriological response using smear microscopy or culture is crucial, as most patients are expected to convert to sputum-negative status within the first few months of treatment. Persistent culture positivity should prompt a review of the regimen and DST performance. National TB programs should aim for complete registration of MDR/RR-TB patients and regular review of cohort data. Active pharmacovigilance is essential, especially with the increasing use of new and repurposed medications in MDR/RR-TB regimens. Accurate data collection using electronic registers is strongly advised to inform policy revisions and improve patient outcomes. For patients with isoniazid-resistant TB, a 6-month regimen of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin is recommended. Streptomycin or other injectable agents should not be added to the regimen. The evidence supporting this recommendation is based on individual patient data analysis, which showed higher treatment success rates with 6-month regimens compared to longer ones. The addition of streptomycin did not significantly reduce mortality, and prolonged use of pyrazinamide was associated with hepatotoxicity. A 6-month regimen without injectable agents is likely to improve health equity and patient outcomes.
